payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Compared with the source image, has the edited image been fully transformed into a drawing made from chalk, rather than only partially stylized toward that appearance?
node.criteria: Pass only if the source-to-edit change makes the image as a whole read as a chalk-made drawing, with the requested transformation complete. Fail if the image remains substantially photographic or otherwise shows only a partial chalk-style conversion, even when some chalk-like texture or shading is evident. Unknown if either image is unavailable or the evidence is insufficient to judge the degree of transformation.
node.binding: Compare the source and edited images to assess the extent and completeness of the requested chalk-drawing transformation; judge the overall result, not isolated chalk-like cues, and do not require a particular visual recipe.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image has been transformed throughout into a soft, grainy chalk-like drawing: the giraffes, trees, ground, and sky all have smudged, textured strokes and muted chalk shading rather than the source's photographic detail.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s evidence supports a complete transformation: the edited scene is broadly rendered with grainy, smudged chalk-like strokes, including the giraffes, foliage, ground, and sky, rather than retaining the source’s photographic appearance. Yet the aggregate is `yes` while the reference is `partial`; the question and criteria already distinguish complete from partial conversion, so do not weaken that threshold or treat low confidence as evidence of missing edits. Investigate the decision-to-label mapping and whether the node is actually asked to emit the rubric’s three-way outcome: a binary pass/fail check may map this positive trace to `yes` even when the aggregate expects `partial`. Keep the source/edit comparison and whole-image criterion, but make the binding or routing preserve the distinction between some progress and full completion. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated."}
